Evidence clusters into two camps: large meta-analyses (d1) report no overall increased cancer risk from night-shift work, while other sources (d2, d3, d4) identify probable carcinogenicity for certain cancers (e.g., breast) and mechanistic plausibility. The literature presents conflicting conclusions about whether shift work increases cancer risk. A large meta-analysis of 57 publications covering 8.5 million participants found no overall increase in cancer risk from night-shift work, including among rotating and fixed night workers [d1]. In contrast, authoritative reviews and evaluations report that shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms is probably carcinogenic to humans, with high confidence that persistent night shift work can cause breast cancer [d2]. Experimental evidence further suggests night shifts disrupt rhythms in cancer-related genes and increase vulnerability to DNA damage [d3]. Observational studies also link long-term rotating night shifts to higher colorectal cancer risk [d4]. However, a single report notes increased lung cancer mortality among women working rotating night shifts for more than 15 years [d5], and a general review flags cancer as a likely consequence of shift work without quantifying overall risk [d6].

Given these divergent findings—null overall risk versus elevated risks for specific cancers and mechanistic plausibility—the evidence supports the conclusion that research outcomes on shift work and cancer risk are conflicting.
